paragraphs: Anomaly detection asks whether an observation belongs to the usual pattern of data or falls outside it. This paper shows that the task can be interpreted as binary classification. That interpretation connects the problem of identifying unusual observations to methods designed to distinguish between two categories.

The authors use this connection to propose a support vector machine for anomaly detection. The contribution is therefore both a reformulation of the learning problem and a method built from that reformulation. It gives a classification-based route to anomaly detection, with theoretical analysis accompanying the proposed algorithm.

The theoretical results include consistency and learning rates, addressing how the method behaves as more data become available and how rapidly learning progresses. The paper also compares the proposed method experimentally with the standard one-class SVM. Together, these contributions connect the classification interpretation to mathematical guarantees and an established practical alternative; the supplied abstract does not state which method performs better in that comparison.
neurips-2004-density-level-detection-is-.tldr: The paper recasts anomaly detection as binary classification and develops an SVM with consistency and learning-rate results.

paragraphs: Linear Discriminant Analysis extracts features and reduces dimensionality for tasks such as face recognition. A version based on QR decomposition, LDA/QR, offers competitive classification accuracy with substantially lower time and storage costs than other LDA methods. Its linear projection, however, may be unsuitable when the data have nonlinear structure.

The paper introduces KDA/QR, which extends the QR-based approach using a kernel operator to handle nonlinear data. It then develops AKDA/QR, an efficient approximation of that extension. The two steps address related needs: broadening the structures the method can represent and making the resulting computation more economical.

On face image data, both versions achieve classification accuracy competitive with Generalized Discriminant Analysis, the kernel discriminant method used for comparison. The approximate version also has much lower time and space costs. These findings support the practical value of approximation in the tested setting: it retains competitive classification performance while reducing the computational burden of nonlinear feature extraction.
neurips-2004-efficient-kernel-discrimina.tldr: A kernel extension of QR-based discriminant analysis, together with an efficient approximation, delivers competitive face classification accuracy at reduced computational cost.

paragraphs: Some probabilistic models are too difficult to analyze exactly, so useful inference depends on approximations. This paper introduces a framework organized around free energy, described here as negative log marginal likelihood. The framework generalizes adaptive TAP and expectation propagation, connecting these approaches through a common construction.

The construction uses two approximating distributions that capture different aspects of the original model, such as constraints on individual nodes and interactions between nodes. They are required to agree on selected moments, which are numerical summaries of their distributions. This allows the approximations to represent different information while remaining consistent on the summaries chosen to connect them.

The authors test the framework on a difficult problem with binary variables on fully connected graphs and two-dimensional grids. They report good performance with moment choices corresponding either to separate nodes or to a spanning-tree structure. The Bethe approximation performs much worse in these tests, including on grids. The result highlights the usefulness of the proposed consistency construction for these benchmark models.
neurips-2004-expectation-consistent-free.tldr: The paper builds approximate inference methods from two distributions that agree on selected moments and reports good performance on binary graphical-model benchmarks.

paragraphs: The paper studies decision making when the rewards attached to actions and states can change at every step, potentially through adversarial choices. The environment's transition dynamics remain fixed. This separates uncertainty about what will be rewarding from changes in how actions move the agent through the environment.

The performance target is the reward that the best stationary policy would have achieved over time. A stationary policy uses the same decision rule throughout play. Regret measures the agent's shortfall relative to this reference, allowing the authors to ask how well an adaptive agent can compete despite changing rewards.

The authors provide efficient algorithms with regret bounds that do not depend on the number of states. Instead, the bounds depend on a particular horizon time of the process and only logarithmically on the number of actions. They also show computational hardness when the dynamics change over time. Fixed dynamics are thus a substantive condition of the positive result, rather than an incidental modeling choice.
neurips-2004-experts-in-a-markov-decisio.tldr: With fixed dynamics and changing rewards, efficient MDP algorithms achieve regret bounds independent of the number of states, while changing dynamics make the problem computationally hard.

paragraphs: Regularization controls how strongly a fitted model is constrained, helping address overfitting that can damage prediction and interpretation. Changing its strength produces a sequence of different optimal models. This paper studies how to follow that sequence incrementally as the regularization setting changes.

The proposed general algorithm uses second-order approximations to track the path of regularized solutions. Such approximations represent local curvature, allowing the procedure to account for a solution path that bends as the regularization varies. The computational aim is to move through related solutions in an organized way, taking advantage of their connection along the path.

The authors prove that, under mild conditions, the algorithm stays very close to the path of optimal solutions, and they illustrate the approach with examples. This is a conditional approximation guarantee, rather than a claim that every computed point is exactly optimal. Its significance is that incremental path following receives theoretical support as a flexible way to explore regularized fits.
neurips-2004-following-curved-regularize.tldr: A general algorithm uses second-order approximations to follow curved regularization paths and, under mild conditions, stays close to the optimal solutions.

paragraphs: Evidence that perception follows Bayesian principles raises a mechanistic question: how could networks of spiking neurons perform the required inference? This paper constructs recurrent networks of noisy integrate-and-fire neurons that carry out approximate Bayesian inference for dynamic and hierarchical graphical models.

The proposed connection uses changes in neuronal membrane potential to implement belief propagation in logarithmic form. A neuron's probability of firing approximates the posterior probability of its preferred state, given earlier inputs. Neural activity therefore has a probabilistic interpretation: firing likelihood represents the model's updated belief about a particular state.

Two examples illustrate the construction. In a motion network, a direction-selective neuron's firing probability becomes proportional to the posterior probability of motion in its preferred direction. A two-level hierarchical network produces attentional effects resembling observations in visual areas V2 and V4. These examples support a possible neural implementation of approximate inference and offer a Bayesian interpretation of attentional modulation, without establishing that biological circuits necessarily use this mechanism.
neurips-2004-hierarchical-bayesian-infer.tldr: Recurrent networks of noisy spiking neurons implement approximate Bayesian inference and reproduce examples of motion coding and attention-related effects.

paragraphs: A large Gaussian mixture represents a distribution through many component distributions. This paper asks how to replace that model with a smaller mixture while preserving its component structure. The proposed approach groups the original components, making model reduction itself a clustering problem.

The algorithm minimizes a new distance measure between Gaussian mixtures. That measure is easy to compute and has a motivation based on a suitable stochastic model. Crucially, each iteration operates directly on the mixture's parameters. The procedure therefore avoids explicitly drawing a new set of data points from the model to carry out the reduction.

The authors demonstrate the method through hierarchical clustering of scenery images and handwritten digits. These applications show how grouping components can produce progressively coarser organization while working with an existing probabilistic representation. The central contribution is an efficient route from a detailed mixture to a smaller one, using a computationally accessible objective and parameter-based updates to retain the original model's component organization.
neurips-2004-hierarchical-clustering-of-.tldr: The paper reduces Gaussian mixtures by clustering their components using an easily computed distance and updates that require no explicit data resampling.

paragraphs: Image structure depends on interactions among pixels, including relationships involving more than a pair. Classical higher-order moments and spectra can describe such relationships, but images create an enormous number of terms to estimate and interpret. This paper proposes another way to represent those interactions.

The method expresses multiplicative pixel interactions through a series of Wiener functionals. It estimates those functionals implicitly using polynomial kernels, avoiding the combinatorial growth associated with explicitly handling classical higher-order statistics. The key methodological change is how the interactions are computed: the representation can incorporate them without enumerating the full collection of statistical terms.

Initial results show correct prediction of structures such as lines and corners. They also indicate that interactions involving up to five pixels play an important role in natural images. These findings suggest that higher-order relationships carry useful structural information and that the implicit approach can make that information accessible. The abstract presents these as early results, rather than a comprehensive account of every relevant image interaction.
neurips-2004-implicit-wiener-series-for-.tldr: Implicit Wiener-series estimation with polynomial kernels captures higher-order pixel interactions without explicitly enumerating the full set of statistical terms.

paragraphs: Tracking an object from one camera involves several coupled unknowns: its three-dimensional position and orientation, changes in shape, and the appearance of both object and background. This paper introduces a generative model and stochastic filtering algorithm that estimate these quantities together.

The authors show that the task is formally equivalent to filtering a conditionally Gaussian process. Their method samples the nonlinear object-motion component using Monte Carlo techniques, then filters object and background textures exactly conditional on each sampled motion. This division gives different parts of the tracking problem computational treatments suited to their mathematical structure.

To guide importance sampling, the algorithm uses Laplace's method and exploits smoothness across space and time in image sequences. The resulting framework includes optic flow and template-based tracking as special cases and clarifies conditions under which they are optimal. An application to three-dimensional non-rigid face tracking demonstrates the combined model. The contribution connects a practical joint tracker with a broader probabilistic explanation of familiar tracking methods.
neurips-2004-joint-tracking-of-pose-expr.tldr: A single-camera tracker samples nonlinear motion while filtering textures exactly conditional on motion, unifying pose, deformation, and appearance estimation.

paragraphs: Learning from examples and regularizing ill-posed inverse problems have long been recognized as closely related. This paper addresses a stronger question: whether learning can formally be expressed as an inverse problem, and whether regularization theory can independently produce results normally associated with learning theory.

The authors establish this connection for learning with square loss. They translate the learning task into the language of regularization theory and study a discretization of the corresponding inverse problem. Discretization supplies the mathematical route by which the inverse-problem formulation yields conclusions about learning from examples.

Through this formulation, the paper derives consistency results and an optimal choice of regularization parameter. Consistency concerns the behavior of learning as the available evidence grows, while parameter choice determines how regularization enters the procedure. The significance is a formal bridge that makes tools from one theory productive in the other. The square-loss setting is part of the stated result, so the abstract's conclusion should be read within that scope.
neurips-2004-learning-regularization-and.tldr: For square loss, the paper formally casts learning as an inverse problem and derives consistency and optimal regularization choices through regularization theory.

paragraphs: Semantic taxonomies organize knowledge through relationships such as one category being a kind of another. Building and maintaining resources such as WordNet requires substantial effort. This paper develops an algorithm that learns these hypernym, or is-a, relationships automatically from text.

Earlier approaches used a small collection of manually written text patterns. The proposed method generalizes that idea using dependency paths extracted from sentence parse trees. Given training text containing known hypernym pairs, it identifies useful grammatical connections between the words. It then applies the learned paths to new corpora to discover additional pairs.

The evaluation asks whether two nouns in a news article stand in a hypernym relationship. On that task, the automatically extracted database achieves both higher precision and higher recall than WordNet: its identified relationships are more accurate, and it captures more of the relevant relationships. This supports the usefulness of learned syntactic patterns for extending lexical knowledge, with the reported advantage tied to the specific evaluation task.
neurips-2004-learning-syntactic-patterns.tldr: Learning grammatical dependency patterns enables automatic hypernym discovery, with higher precision and recall than WordNet on the reported news-article task.

paragraphs: Scanned handwritten manuscripts contain searchable language, but the writing must be connected to text before full-text search is possible. This paper uses a generalized hidden Markov model to make a medieval Latin manuscript searchable, combining evidence about letter appearance with evidence about Latin letter sequences.

The transition model is learned from transcribed Latin, while the emission model uses one example of each of 22 letters. The authors report results for unigram, bigram, and trigram models, exploring different amounts of sequence context. This separates the source of linguistic information from the small set of visual letter examples.

On 25 pages of a manuscript of Terence, the method correctly transcribes 75% of letters and produces very strong search results. Examples involving variant spellings show that retrieval follows the actual writing in the document. The model also produces fair searches on a document that supplied no training data. These findings demonstrate that useful manuscript search can coexist with substantial transcription errors.
neurips-2004-making-latin-manuscripts-se.tldr: A generalized hidden Markov model makes handwritten Latin searchable, producing strong retrieval despite correctly transcribing only 75% of letters in the reported manuscript.

paragraphs: Repeated measurements of a process can differ in timing, amplitude, and noise even when they reflect shared underlying structure. Combining them usefully requires aligning those differences. This paper introduces the Continuous Profile Model to learn a common representation and align multiple continuous-valued time series to it.

The model assumes that each observed series comes from one latent trace through non-uniform subsampling, local rescaling, and additive noise. These operations account for varying sampling rates along the trace, changing amplitude, and imperfect observations. Unsupervised training learns a canonical, high-resolution trace that fuses information from the replicates.

Inference then finds the temporal and scale alignment between each observation and that shared trace. The authors successfully apply the method to speech from multiple speakers and to proteomic measurements from Liquid Chromatography–Mass Spectrometry. These applications illustrate how a generative account of variation can support both alignment and fusion, with the shared latent trace serving as the reference that ties the observations together.
neurips-2004-multiple-alignment-of-conti.tldr: The Continuous Profile Model learns a shared high-resolution trace while aligning noisy time series that vary locally in timing and amplitude.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning uses both labeled and unlabeled examples. This paper develops a convex optimization method for constructing kernels that combine those sources of information systematically. Its starting point is the spectral decomposition of a graph Laplacian, which supplies the structure from which the kernel matrix is derived.

The method learns a nonparametric transformation with order constraints, rather than requiring a choice among fixed parametric kernel families such as diffusion or Gaussian random field kernels. This provides flexibility in the learned kernel while retaining explicit constraints during optimization. The central aim is to let the construction adapt without first selecting a particular parametric form.

The resulting optimization problem is a quadratically constrained quadratic program, and the authors describe it as computationally feasible for large datasets. They evaluate the learned kernels with support vector machines on real datasets and report encouraging results. The evidence supports the promise of this flexible construction, while the abstract characterizes the empirical outcome qualitatively rather than claiming universal superiority.
neurips-2004-nonparametric-transforms-of.tldr: Convex optimization learns flexible graph-based kernels from labeled and unlabeled data without requiring a fixed parametric kernel family.

paragraphs: A visual cortical neuron receives many inputs from neurons with roughly similar stimulus preferences. This paper asks whether that organization supports efficient sensory-information readout. The authors combine a simple model of neuronal population activity with information-theoretic analysis to investigate the relationship between input selectivity and information transmission.

The model identifies a requirement for efficient transmission: the width of each input neuron's tuning curve should approximately match the spread of preferred stimuli across the neurons supplying the target. These are distinct quantities. One describes how broadly an individual neuron responds, while the other describes how diverse the input population's preferences are.

A meta-analysis of neurophysiological data finds this approximate match for connections between cortical neurons in visual cortex. The authors therefore suggest that the organization of these inputs in V1 allows optimal information transmission. The biological conclusion is a suggestion supported by agreement between the model's requirement and the analyzed measurements; it is not presented as proof that every cortical input arrangement is optimal.
neurips-2004-optimal-information-decodin.tldr: Modeling and a neurophysiological meta-analysis suggest that matching individual tuning widths to population preference spread supports efficient information transmission in V1.

paragraphs: Determining a protein structure from X-ray crystallography includes interpreting a three-dimensional electron density map. This pattern-finding step can take substantial time. The paper introduces DEFT, a deformable-template algorithm intended to automate that interpretation by matching a flexible protein model to the map.

DEFT builds its model from the protein's amino-acid sequence using pictorial structures. This representation gives the matching procedure a structured but flexible object to fit into the observed density. The paper also extends the pictorial-structure matching algorithm to support the requirements of automated density-map interpretation.

The authors test DEFT on density maps with resolutions from 2 to 4 Å and report root-mean-squared errors from 1.38 to 1.84 Å. These results provide a quantitative demonstration of the approach on the tested maps. The main significance is the connection between molecular modeling and structured visual matching: sequence information defines the protein model, while the density map supplies the spatial evidence used to position that flexible structure.
neurips-2004-pictorial-structures-for-mo.tldr: DEFT fits a flexible protein model built from its amino-acid sequence into electron density maps to automate crystallographic interpretation.

paragraphs: Planning with uncertain action outcomes is often slower than planning in a deterministic world. Yet some tasks have uncertainty only at a few points: long predictable action sequences are interrupted by sensing actions with uncertain results. This paper focuses on that sparse pattern of stochasticity.

The proposed algorithm, MDP Compression Planning, combines A* search with value iteration to solve stochastic shortest-path problems. Its design brings together a method suited to deterministic planning and one suited to uncertain outcomes. The motivation is to exploit predictable stretches of a task while still accounting for the uncertain decisions embedded within it.

Experiments simulate a ground robot cooperating with a helicopter to complete a partial map and reach a goal. In these domains with sparse uncertainty, the algorithm can run substantially faster than competing planners. The finding supports tailoring planning computation to where uncertainty occurs. Its reported speed advantage is tied to the tested sparse-uncertainty domains, rather than asserted for arbitrary Markov decision processes.
neurips-2004-planning-for-markov-decisio.tldr: MDP Compression Planning combines A* and value iteration to accelerate stochastic shortest-path planning in domains where uncertain outcomes are sparse.

paragraphs: Spectral clustering must decide how strongly data points resemble one another and how many groups to extract. These decisions become difficult when groups have different scales or sit within irregular background clutter. This paper addresses those issues together with automatic selection of the number of clusters.

The authors propose computing pairwise affinities using local scales. This makes the similarity calculation responsive to the surroundings of the points being compared. They report better clustering from this local scaling, especially for data containing multiple scales and for clusters embedded in cluttered backgrounds.

The method also uses structure in the eigenvectors to infer the number of groups automatically. The resulting algorithm eliminates the final randomly initialized k-means stage. Together, these changes address both the construction of the similarity representation and the extraction of groups from it. The contribution is an adaptive spectral-clustering procedure that handles the highlighted difficulties while reducing reliance on a separately initialized final grouping step.
neurips-2004-self-tuning-spectral-cluste.tldr: Local affinity scales and eigenvector structure improve spectral clustering across varying scales and clutter while enabling automatic group-count inference.

paragraphs: A low-dimensional representation can support density modeling, dimensionality reduction, and visualization, but it must still describe the distribution of the observations. This paper introduces a semi-parametric latent-variable method designed to represent data whose underlying low-dimensional distribution may contain multiple modes.

The method estimates the latent distribution nonparametrically, giving it flexibility to capture several concentrations of probability in the hidden representation. It also allows model components from the exponential family. This second choice makes the approach suitable for different observation types, including binary values and counts, within the same broad modeling framework.

Simulations on real-valued, binary, and count data show favorable comparisons with related methods in separating populations and generalizing to unseen samples. These findings address both the organization of the learned representation and its usefulness beyond the observations used to fit it. The contribution combines flexibility in the hidden distribution with flexibility in the type of data being modeled, rather than relying on a single observation format.
neurips-2004-semi-parametric-exponential.tldr: A semi-parametric latent-variable model combines a nonparametric hidden distribution with exponential-family components to handle multimodal real-valued, binary, and count data.

paragraphs: Efficient sensory coding often emphasizes removing redundancy from inputs. This paper argues that noise changes the objective: redundant information can help compensate for an imprecise neural representation. It proposes a model that balances redundancy reduction with useful repetition when individual units have limited capacity.

Under these noisy, limited-capacity conditions, the optimal representation becomes overcomplete and spans multiple scales. Overcompleteness means that the population can contain more units than the intrinsic dimensionality of the input. This permits a population to reconstruct information precisely even when the representation supplied by any one unit is imprecise.

Like earlier models, the proposed model accounts for the localized and oriented structure of simple cells. It also predicts a different population organization that agrees more closely with physiological data than previous models. These results offer a theoretical perspective on why neuron numbers expand from the retina to V1. The explanatory force comes from treating limited capacity and noise as constraints that can make redundancy useful.
neurips-2004-sparse-coding-of-natural-im.tldr: With noisy, limited-capacity units, a model balancing compression and useful redundancy favors overcomplete, multiscale representations closer to physiological observations.

paragraphs: Classification methods must sometimes learn from input measurements corrupted by noise. This paper treats that corruption as uncertainty to be incorporated into the learning model. It develops a general statistical framework for the problem and uses that reasoning to reformulate support vector classification.

The resulting classifier allows uncertainty in the inputs as part of its formulation. The authors also derive a geometric interpretation, connecting the statistical construction to an intuitive view of the classification problem. They develop algorithms to solve the formulation efficiently, linking the proposed modeling change to a practical computational procedure.

Empirical results show the new method outperforming the standard SVM on the noisy-input problems studied. This supports the usefulness of representing input uncertainty explicitly in those settings. The paper's contribution spans the statistical model, its geometric meaning, and the algorithms needed to fit it; the performance finding is empirical evidence for the tested problems rather than a guarantee for every possible kind of noise.
neurips-2004-support-vector-classificati.tldr: A statistical reformulation of support vector classification explicitly accommodates input uncertainty and outperforms a standard SVM on the reported noisy-input problems.

paragraphs: Classical conditioning involves learning responses to predictive events, and useful behavior can depend on responding at the right moment. This paper implements a biophysically constrained cerebellar model on a neuromorphic analog VLSI chip. The model controls adaptive behavior by learning to predict the precise timing of events.

The authors describe the chip's operation and evaluate its learning in two settings: circuit-level simulations of conditioning and behavioral experiments with a mobile robot. These evaluations connect the circuitry's learning behavior to its use in an acting system, where a conditioned response must be coordinated with events outside the chip.

The reported results demonstrate both acquisition and extinction of adaptively timed conditioned responses under real-world conditions, with ultra-low power consumption. Acquisition shows that the system can learn the response, while extinction shows that the learned behavior can diminish through conditioning experience. The contribution is a hardware realization of a cerebellar learning model that combines timing-sensitive adaptation with low-power operation in a physical robotic setting.
neurips-2004-the-cerebellum-chip-an-anal.tldr: A low-power analog cerebellum chip learns and extinguishes precisely timed conditioned responses in simulations and mobile-robot experiments.

paragraphs: An SVM's cost parameter affects which fitted solution is obtained, and this paper argues that choosing it can be critical. Studying that choice therefore involves understanding how the solution changes as the parameter varies. The paper makes this family of solutions the central computational object.

The authors derive an algorithm that fits the entire regularization path, covering every value of the cost parameter. A path represents the relationship between parameter settings and their associated SVM solutions. Computing it provides access to the full family of fits, extending the scope of a single training procedure beyond one selected setting.

The striking stated result is that this full-path calculation has essentially the same computational cost as fitting one SVM model. That claim makes comprehensive exploration of parameter-dependent solutions computationally appealing. The algorithm addresses the cost of obtaining the available fits; the abstract's motivation remains that the parameter choice matters. Its contribution is an efficient way to expose the full range of solutions relevant to that choice.
neurips-2004-the-entire-regularization-p.tldr: The paper derives an algorithm for the full SVM regularization path at essentially the computational cost of fitting a single SVM.

paragraphs: Clustering can be studied by comparing probability distributions associated with groups of data. This paper introduces the Laplacian pdf distance, a measure between probability density functions. It connects that measure to kernel learning through Parzen-window density estimation, linking a statistical comparison to a geometric representation.

In a kernel feature space defined by the eigenspectrum of the Laplacian data matrix, the measure corresponds to the cosine of the angle between cluster mean vectors. This gives the density comparison a concrete geometric interpretation: it relates to the directions of group averages in the constructed feature space.

The Laplacian data matrix and its eigenspectrum can be obtained automatically from the available data through optimal Parzen-window selection. The authors also interpret the distance as a risk function connected to error probability. Together, these results tie density estimation, kernel geometry, and statistical risk into one clustering objective. The contribution is this mathematical connection and data-based construction, rather than an empirical claim about outperforming particular clustering algorithms.
neurips-2004-the-laplacian-pdf-distance-.tldr: The Laplacian pdf distance links density comparisons to angles between cluster means in a kernel feature space and to a risk interpretation involving error probability.

paragraphs: Human Interactive Proofs are challenges intended to distinguish people from computers by presenting tasks that computers supposedly find difficult. This paper studies such systems to identify weaknesses in machine learning through tasks where humans retain an advantage. The authors examine several available visual challenges.

They find that most of the studied systems rely on recognition alone and can be defeated easily with machine learning. Harder systems combine recognition with segmentation: the computer must work out which image portions form separate items as well as identify them. Within their investigation, constructing segmentation challenges proves the most effective way to confuse the learning algorithms.

The authors use this observation to build effective challenges deployed in MSN Passport and to design difficult segmentation tasks for machine learning research. The findings connect practical challenge design with an analysis of what makes a visual task hard for the studied algorithms. The reported lesson concerns those systems and methods, rather than establishing that segmentation will remain a permanent barrier to automated recognition.
neurips-2004-using-machine-learning-to-b.tldr: The study finds segmentation more challenging than recognition alone for the examined machine-learning systems and uses that insight to design deployed human-verification challenges.
